newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bayern-Hypo faces slow 1997 earnings growth.
newsitem.headline: Bayern-Hypo faces slow 1997 earnings growth.

text.p: Germany's fifth largest listed bank, Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank AG, on Tuesday predicted a rise in operating earnings this year after a decline in 1996 but its profit growth is expected to lag that of its domestic rivals.

Hypo-Bank, regarded as a potential takeover candidate, said operating profit before bad debt provisions grew at a slightly faster pace in the first four months than in the first quarter when it rose 1.5 percent.
The slow earnings growth contrasts with profit gains of between 10 percent and 21 percent at its four bigger competitors Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank, Commerzbank and Bayerische Vereinsbank.
Hypo-Bank is now likely to play catch up for the remainder of 1997 and should at best turn in a modest rise in operating profit, analysts said.
"Hypo-Bank is likely to lag the competition for the rest of the year because its interest income in the first three months was poor," said Olaf Conrad, banking analyst at Morgan Stanley.
Speaking at Hypo-Bank's annual shareholder meeting, chief executive Eberhard Martini reiterated that he could not rule out a capital increase in 1997 or 1998.

"We have not planned one but the possibility cannot be ruled out," Martini said. Hypo-Bank's core capital ratio fell to 4.9 percent in 1996 after it raised its stake in British fund manager Foreign & Colonial to 65 percent from 50 percent.
Capital adequacy was also hit by expansion in mortgage lending in the final months of 1996.

First-quarter net interest income fell 7.8 percent to 1.06 billion marks while net commission income and trading profits rose sharply, by 51.2 percent and 72.2 percent respectively. The bank said interest income developed positively in April.

Analysts said the fall in interest income resulted from the bank's move to curb its non-mortgage lending in a bid to reduce its risk exposure after being hit by losses at several of its industrial shareholdings including Brau und Brunnen.
The management faced heavy criticism at Tuesday's meeting over what one shareholder termed its "scandalous" industrial policy.
Hypo-Bank's shares closed up 0.15 marks at 58.55 marks on Tuesday.

They have risen 57 percent since July last year when market speculation about mergers and takeovers took hold of the German banking sector following Deutsche's disclosure it had a 5.21 percent stake in Vereinsbank.
That prompted market talk that Dresdner, Germany's number two bank after Deutsche, may join forces with Hypo-Bank.
Stefan Ermisch, bank analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank, said Hypo-Bank's shares were not cheap at current levels and that he did not expect them to outperform the rest of the banking sector.

"From a fundamental point of view the shares are not cheap, it's the expectation of consolidation in the sector that is underpinning the price," said Ermisch, who has an "underweight" rating on the shares.

Chief executive Eberhard Martini said the bank had made progress in reducing its exposure to problem loans but added that, given the sluggish economy and high corporate insolvencies, there was no reason to sound the all-clear on banks' risk exposure.
The real estate market in particular, where Hypo-Bank has a high market share, was showing no signs of an upturn, he added.
"We are confident that we have made a significant step forward in overcoming our problem loan cases, as is being signalled by falling risk quotas in most loan areas."
Hypo-Bank in 1996 sustained an 8.7 percent drop in operating profit after risk provisions to 1.19 billion marks.
